title: Seeing the ox
hook: third picture: he glimpses the ox itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second picture: prints in the mud, signs of the ox found in the teachings. Your line: the tracks. Which sign of the way did you notice? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-three.

A bird sings somewhere in the branches. The sun is warm, the wind is soft, and the willows along the bank are green. That's the scene in the verse for the third oxherding picture, and it's oddly ordinary. No thunder, no vision in the clouds. The herdsman has been following prints for a long time, reading about the ox, talking about the ox. Then, on a pleasant afternoon, he hears that bird, looks up, and there among the willows is the ox itself. Today: seeing the ox.
screen: `A BIRD SINGS. THE WILLOWS ARE GREEN.` → `AN ORDINARY AFTERNOON.` → `THE OX ITSELF.`

segments.voice: First, what changes. Yesterday he had evidence. Today he has contact. The preface for this picture says he finds the way in, in paraphrase, through sound: hearing clearly opens the gate. Reading about honey and tasting it are different kinds of knowing, and this is the move from one to the other. Second, the glimpse comes through the senses, not around them. The verse doesn't take the herdsman somewhere special. It keeps him right where he is: birdsong, sunlight, wind, willows. Some Zen teachers say the way isn't hidden behind daily life; it's shining through it. The verse even asks where the ox could possibly hide. Third, the picture is honest about how much he sees. In some well-known drawings, only part of the ox shows, its head or its hindquarters, the rest still behind a tree. He has seen it. He hasn't caught it. A glimpse can be completely real and still be brief. Fourth, why the glimpse matters. Without it, all the tracks in the world stay secondhand. With it, he knows for himself that the ox is there. In ordinary life, a glimpse can be very small: a moment where the mind is clear and nothing is missing, the sound of rain heard all the way through. It may pass in seconds. The third picture says that's enough to change the search, because now he knows what he's looking for, and the old question, is there even an ox, has been answered.
screen: `FROM EVIDENCE TO CONTACT.` · `THE GLIMPSE COMES THROUGH THE SENSES.` · `SEEN, BUT NOT YET CAUGHT.` · `NOW HE KNOWS FOR HIMSELF.` · then, large: `THERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and let your eyes rest, open or closed. Instead of looking for anything, let sound come to you, the way the bird's song came to the herdsman. The hum of a fridge. A car outside. Your own breath. Hear one sound all the way through, from its start to its fading. If there's a moment where it's simply clear, just this, notice it without grabbing. If nothing like that comes, listening is still the practice. The bell holds the time.
Seeing the ox. The third oxherding picture: through birdsong and sunlight, the herdsman glimpses the ox itself, real, but not yet caught. Today's word.
Your line: there it is. Today, catch one clear moment, a sound, a face, a cup of tea, and quietly say: there it is. Then let it go. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: In Zen communities the third oxherding picture is often read as a first direct glimpse of one's own nature, and teachers use it to remind students that such a glimpse is real but is the start of training, not the end.

fork.setup: you're the herdsman, following prints. a bird sings, you look up, and part of the ox shows behind a tree. what has just happened?
options: you've seen the ox for yourself, but not caught it.
fork.reveal: the third picture is a real glimpse of the ox itself, not secondhand evidence. catching it is still ahead, and tomorrow it fights the rope.

original.note: Chinese (jianniu): 'seeing the ox', the name of the third oxherding picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: seeing the ox is the big finish.
what it means: a real but partial glimpse, the move from reading about the ox to seeing it.
what a scholar hears: the preface opens the gate through hearing, and the verse keeps the glimpse inside an ordinary spring scene, not beyond the senses.

notes: All oxherding material paraphrased. Check: preface for picture 3 links the entry to hearing/sound (the six senses); verse has a bird (oriole/nightingale) singing, warm sun, soft wind, green willows on the bank.
'In many versions of the drawing, only part of the ox shows' describes common illustrations; confirm or soften.
The honey image is illustration, not from the text.
Original 見牛; pronunciation approximates Mandarin jianniu.

Editor: hook no longer has the ox 'half hidden' (the verse asks where it could hide); 'Zen teachers often say' and 'in many versions' softened to 'some'; removed the 'standing in the open' line that contradicted the partial drawing.
